If you have to re-season a pan a self cleaning oven is very useful. Put the pan in and set the cleaning cycle. All the old seasoning will burn off. This won't take care of any rust, if it is a neglected pan or a thrift store find. Soak the pan in vinegar for a few hours or overnight if it is in terrible condition. When your scrub with steel wool it will cut through it easily. I know the page says to set your oven to 400°, but really you only want to go 25° to 50° past the smoking point of the oil you're using. So do your research. I like to only go 25° past and check the pan ever hour to hour and a half. I know this takes longer, but it helps to keep the seasoning from burning and having to repeat the process. after washing and drying thoroughly I put my pan on the shove at a low het to heat up to make sure it is dry. I usually rub it down with a little olive oil, taking care to remove the excess then put it back on the heat for a bit.

I realized I forgot some things after I made this post.

  • when you season the pan and take it out to check it while you're baking it, if the pan hasn't turned black add another layer of oil. Be careful to remove the excess or the pan will become sticky. Make sure you coat the entire pan, handle and bottom included. If your pan is sticky put it back in the oven to bake longer and do not add more oil.
  • there are modern and vintage pans. Modern pans are much easier to season but are not as non stick as a well seasoned vintage pan. The difference is the finish. Vintage pans have a smooth finish, while modern ones have a rough surface. Make the purchase that suits you.
  • Modern pans usually come pre seasoned. The factory seasoning is usually inferior. There is usually no indication of what kind of oil they used either. I reccomend stripping and re-seasoning them immediately before use. Especially if you have any food allergies.
  • The finished seasoning on a vintage pan is usually splotchy. This is because the smooth pans can't absorb the oil as well. Dont worry about it.

Stevie Ray Vaughan - Tin Pan Alley (1980)

While the album was released about two years after Vaughan's death in 1990, the actual performance took place on April 1, 1980 at Steamboat 1874 in Austin, Texas, and was broadcast live on KLBJ-FM radio. A 25-year-old Vaughan, still more than three years away from the release of his first studio album, performs with his "Double Trouble" bandmates: Chris Layton, drummer, and Jackie Newhouse, bassist. (Newhouse was replaced by bassist Tommy Shannon in January 1981, who would remain part of Double Trouble until Stevie's death.)

Plenty of electric blues players can bluster and roar through a performance, but a slow tune, even over a set of straight 12-bar changes, is the style’s ultimate challenge. Tapping into the music’s deepest pools of expression, where delicately squeezed, shaken, and slid notes become stand-ins for a range of human emotions, it takes an outstanding guitarist to sculpt a soulful slow blues. T-Bone Walker, B.B. King, Otis Rush, Buddy Guy, Ronnie Earl, and Stevie Ray Vaughan all have made staggering contributions, but the best recorded slow blues of the past 25 years may be Vaughan’s 1984 rendition of “Tin Pan Alley” on his second album, Couldn’t Stand the Weather.

“Tin Pan Alley” was a staple of Vaughan’s concerts long before he put it on tape. The song was written by R&B tunesmith and performer Bob Geddins, who came from Texas but ultimately settled in the San Francisco Bay Area to become the dean of Oakland’s blues scene.
